transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

I start projects and assignments full of ideas, but I just can’t seem to follow through and finish things, and it’s already cost me my first job. I'm here because I really need to understand why I can't seem to complete tasks reliably despite wanting to.
Have you struggled with these difficulties in finishing tasks and staying organized since you were a child, or is this a more recent issue?

They became a major crisis over the last year when my responsibilities at the startup ramped up, but looking back, I've struggled with this since childhood. Even in elementary school, my report cards always said I was "bright but daydreams, forgets homework, and talks out of turn," and I was constantly losing worksheets and blurting out answers.
Over the past year, since these difficulties became a major crisis, have you also been feeling persistently down, sad, or lost interest in activities you normally enjoy?

I wouldn't say I've felt persistently sad or lost interest in my hobbies, but losing my job was a major blow to my confidence and left me incredibly frustrated. I have pulled back from social activities, but that's really more out of shame and embarrassment over my recent struggles than a lack of interest.
Do you find yourself constantly worrying excessively about many different everyday things—such as your health, family, or finances—and finding it very difficult to control that worry?

No, I wouldn't say I experience that kind of constant, everyday worry. Any stress I have is pretty much entirely focused on my inability to get things done and losing my job, rather than worrying about my health or other general things.

opening_question.question: Hello, I'm glad to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a chronic, lifelong history of inattention (difficulty finishing tasks, disorganization, daydreaming, and losing items) and impulsivity (talking out of turn, blurting out answers) dating back to elementary school. These symptoms have caused significant functional impairment, recently culminating in the loss of their first job. Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) and depressive episode (F32.9) were considered but ruled out, as the patient's anxiety and social withdrawal are situational and secondary to their executive dysfunction and job loss, rather than representing independent, pervasive mood or anxiety disorders.
